skill.name: native-feel-cross-platform-desktop
skill.description: Use when the user is designing, prototyping, or rewriting a desktop app that must run on multiple OSes (macOS + Windows, optionally Linux) AND feel indistinguishable from a native app to its users — fast launch, native windowing, native input handling, native materials. Trigger words include "cross-platform desktop", "Electron alternative", "Tauri vs native", "WebView wrapper", "near-native performance", "Raycast architecture", "WebKit/WebView2 quirks", "WKWebView", "system tray app", "global hotkey app", "launcher app". Do NOT trigger this skill for pure web apps, pure mobile apps, or for greenfield projects that have no native-feel requirement.
skill.summary: Guides architecture and audits for cross-platform desktop apps that need native-feeling performance and platform behavior.
skill.author: yetone

content.value_statement: Cross-platform desktop teams often trade native feel for shared UI speed. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through architecture, WebView, IPC, memory, and launch-readiness checks.
actual_capabilities: Applies a decision tree for native-feel desktop architecture choices.
Explains a four-layer macOS and Windows architecture with native shells, WebViews, Node, and Rust.
Provides WebKit and WebView2 guidance for rendering, animation, lifecycle, and native materials.
Defines IPC patterns using one schema and generated typed clients across runtimes.
Uses a ship-readiness checklist to audit interaction, windowing, visuals, and performance.
Clarifies memory measurements and debugging steps for WebView and Node desktop apps.
limitations: It gives architectural guidance, not a complete working app scaffold.
It focuses on macOS and Windows; Linux support is optional and less detailed.
It assumes teams can maintain native shell code plus shared React and TypeScript.
It does not replace platform documentation or performance profiling on target hardware.

use_cases.title: Audit a Web-Wrapped Desktop App
use_cases.description: Find the visual, input, and windowing issues that make an Electron or Tauri app feel like a website.

use_cases.title: Choose a Cross-Platform Architecture
use_cases.description: Decide whether a native shell, system WebView, Node backend, and Rust core fit project constraints.

use_cases.title: Prepare a Native-Feel Ship Review
use_cases.description: Run readiness checks for launch behavior, keyboard handling, materials, memory, and platform conventions.

prompt_templates.title: Audit My App Feel
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of an existing desktop app.
prompt_templates.prompt: My desktop app runs on macOS and Windows but feels like a web app. Use this skill to run the native-feel checklist and give prioritized fixes.

prompt_templates.title: Pick the Right Stack
prompt_templates.scenario: Architecture selection for a new project.
prompt_templates.prompt: I am starting a desktop app that must feel native on macOS and Windows. Run the decision tree and recommend the architecture with trade-offs.

prompt_templates.title: Plan the IPC Boundary
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me design the IPC contract between native shell, WebView, Node backend, and Rust core. Focus on schema ownership and generated clients.

prompt_templates.title: Review WebView Performance Risks
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced performance and platform behavior review.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my WebView desktop architecture for launch latency, hidden-window throttling, animation flicker, memory accounting, and native material integration.

output_examples.input: My Electron app feels web-like on macOS. Where should I start?
output: Start with the ship-readiness checklist, especially cursor behavior, native sheets, system accent color, and platform materials.
Keep Electron if the goal is good enough polish, but expect a ceiling on native window behavior and material fidelity.
Measure the gap with a short user-visible audit before considering a rewrite.

output_examples.input: Should a new launcher use native UI or a shared React WebView?
output: Use the decision tree first: cold-start target, memory floor, extension needs, team skills, and delivery runway matter.
Choose native UI when sub-100ms launch or very low memory is mandatory.
Choose the hybrid architecture when shared iteration speed and extensions justify the WebView and Node baseline.

output_examples.input: Our memory looks high in Activity Monitor.
output: Separate memory pressure from resident size before changing architecture.
Check dirty memory hotspots, then profile WebView, Node, and Rust separately.
Avoid migrating features to native only to reduce a number users may not perceive.

best_practices: Run the decision tree before recommending this architecture.
Keep platform-owned behavior in native shell code and shared product UI in React.
Use one declared IPC schema and generate typed clients for each runtime.
anti_patterns: Choosing Electron or Tauri only because they sound lighter or easier.
Hand-writing IPC types separately in Swift, C#, TypeScript, and Rust.
Optimizing memory numbers before checking memory pressure and user-visible latency.

faq.question: Does this skill build the desktop app for me?
faq.answer: No. It provides architecture guidance, checklists, and review criteria for teams building the app.

faq.question: Which platforms does it cover best?
faq.answer: It focuses on macOS and Windows, with optional Linux considerations depending on the project.

faq.question: Is this only for Raycast-style launchers?
faq.answer: No. Launchers are a strong fit, but the patterns also help productivity tools and resident desktop apps.

faq.question: Can it help improve an existing Electron app?
faq.answer: Yes. It can identify native-feel gaps before a team decides whether a rewrite is justified.

faq.question: Why does the skill discuss WebViews?
faq.answer: It treats the system WebView as a shared rendering surface while native code owns platform behavior.

faq.question: Does it replace performance profiling?
faq.answer: No. It helps choose what to measure, but teams still need profiling on real target machines.
